metadata.title: The Strange Case of Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde
metadata.author: Robert Louis Stevenson

curator_statement.human_truth: Every person contains multitudes — impulses we act on and impulses we suppress. Stevenson gave form to the terrifying idea that the darkness inside us isn’t a flaw to be fixed, but a fundamental part of who we are. Jekyll doesn’t become Hyde; he already IS Hyde. The potion just removes the mask.
curator_statement.historical_moment: Written in 1886, during the height of Victorian respectability, when gentlemen were expected to be moral pillars in public while London’s underworld thrived in shadow. Stevenson wrote the entire novella in three feverish days, burned the first draft, and rewrote it in three more. It became an instant sensation — selling 40,000 copies in six months — because it said out loud what everyone secretly knew: the respectable facade was a lie.
curator_statement.living_relevance: In an age of curated social media personas, where everyone projects a polished self while hiding their darker impulses, Jekyll and Hyde is more relevant than ever. We all maintain a public face and a private one. The story asks: what happens when the gap between who we pretend to be and who we actually are becomes unbridgeable?
curator_statement.invitation: This isn’t a long read — it’s a short, sharp shock. In just five scenes, you’ll follow the mystery of a sinister door, a trampled child, and a will that leaves everything to a man no one has ever seen. By the time you reach the final revelation, you’ll understand why this story invented a phrase that’s been part of our language for nearly 140 years. Everyone has a Hyde. Come meet yours.
curator_statement.one_line: The story that gave us the language to talk about the darkness hiding inside every respectable person.

style_guide.art_style: Dark Victorian noir with ink wash textures — heavy shadows, gaslit atmosphere, influenced by Mike Mignola and Dave McKean
color_palette: Sickly amber (#D4A847) — gaslight and moral corruption
Blood crimson (#8B0000) — violence and Hyde's presence
Cold blue-grey (#6B7B8D) — Jekyll's repression and clinical detachment
Ivory white (#F5F0E1) — innocence and the facade of respectability
style_guide.mood: Oppressive, claustrophobic Victorian dread — the constant sense that something monstrous lurks beneath the veneer of respectability. Shadows are alive, fog obscures truth, and every gentleman's face hides a beast.

character_designs.appearance: Tall, handsome man of 50 with refined features, greying temples, kind but haunted eyes. Carries himself with impeccable posture that slowly deteriorates.
character_designs.clothing: Immaculate dark frock coat, high collar, silk cravat. His clothing becomes increasingly disheveled as the story progresses.
distinguishing_features: Trembling hands he tries to hide
A warmth in his smile that doesn't reach his eyes

character_designs.appearance: Small, pale, dwarfish figure that radiates wrongness. Features are not deformed but give an impression of deformity — something fundamentally off about his proportions.
character_designs.clothing: Jekyll's clothes hanging loose on his smaller frame. Rumpled, stained. Wears a heavy cape to hide in shadows.
distinguishing_features: Movements that are too quick, almost insectile
A shadow that seems larger than his body

character_designs.appearance: Lean, long, dusty, dreary lawyer. Rugged face weathered by years of keeping others' secrets. Loyal eyes.
character_designs.clothing: Conservative dark suit, always proper. A man who blends into the background by design.

style_guide.environment_notes: Victorian London rendered in heavy shadow and fog. Streets are narrow, gaslit corridors. Jekyll's house is grand but with one wing perpetually dark. Hyde's Soho apartment is cramped, stained. The laboratory door is always in shadow — a threshold between worlds.
style_guide.typography_notes: Dialogue in clean serif (Caslon-style). Narration in slightly weathered italic. Hyde's speech in a more jagged, unsettling variant. Sound effects hand-lettered with ink splatter.
consistency_rules: Hyde is ALWAYS drawn smaller than everyone around him
Gaslight casts amber; moonlight casts blue-grey
Jekyll's hands are prominent in every scene — trembling, clenching, transforming
Shadows grow longer and more distorted as the story progresses
The laboratory door appears in the background of at least one panel per scene
Weather worsens with narrative tension — mist to fog to storm

panel_scripts.layout_notes: Wide establishing shot followed by tight conversation panels. The door should dominate the final panel.

panels.visual_direction: Wide shot: A foggy London street at dusk. Mr. Utterson and Mr. Enfield walk side by side, silhouettes against amber gaslight. Victorian buildings loom on either side, their upper floors lost in mist.
panels.narration: Mr. Utterson the lawyer was a man of rugged countenance, that was never lighted by a smile. And yet somehow, he was lovable.

panels.visual_direction: Medium shot of Enfield gesturing toward a sinister door set into a windowless wall. The door is blistered, stained — utterly out of place on the respectable street. Deep shadows pool around its threshold.
dialogue: Did you ever remark that door?
It is connected in my mind with a very odd story.

panels.visual_direction: Flashback panel — tilted angle, more expressionistic. A small, pale figure (Hyde) tramples over a screaming child at a street corner. The scene is rendered in harsh crimson and black. Hyde's face is obscured by shadow but his posture radiates malice.
panels.narration: It was some damned Juggernaut — the man trampled calmly over the child's body and left her screaming on the ground.

panels.visual_direction: Close-up of the sinister door, now filling the entire panel. The wood grain seems to form a face. A keyhole glints like an eye. Utterson's reflection is barely visible in the dark wood.
dialogue: And the man who did this — he had a key to that door.

panel_scripts.layout_notes: Claustrophobic panels that grow tighter as Utterson hunts through the night. The final panel opens wide for the confrontation.

panels.visual_direction: Utterson alone in his study at night, holding Jekyll's will by candlelight. The document glows amber. His face is deeply troubled, carved by shadows. Behind him, bookshelves recede into darkness.
panels.narration: That evening, Mr. Utterson came home to his bachelor house in sombre spirits and sat down to dinner without relish.

panels.visual_direction: Montage panel: Three small frames showing Utterson haunting the street near the door at different times — dawn, noon, night. Each time the street is emptier, the shadows deeper. He is a dark sentinel, watching.
panels.narration: If he be Mr. Hyde, I shall be Mr. Seek.

panels.visual_direction: The confrontation: Hyde emerges from the door, face half-lit by a distant gaslight. He is small but radiates menace. Utterson blocks his path. The size difference is stark — Hyde looks up at the tall lawyer, but somehow Utterson seems the more vulnerable.
dialogue: That is my name. What do you want?

panels.visual_direction: Extreme close-up of Hyde's face — the only time we see it clearly. Not deformed, but deeply wrong. His smile is too wide, his eyes too bright, something reptilian in his gaze. The amber gaslight makes his skin look sickly.
dialogue: Will you let me see your face?
panels.narration: Mr. Hyde was pale and dwarfish; he gave an impression of deformity without any nameable malformation.

panel_scripts.layout_notes: This is the violent centerpiece. Panels shatter and overlap as the murder unfolds. Strict panel borders dissolve into chaos.

panels.visual_direction: A peaceful moonlit scene: Sir Danvers Carew, a beautiful old gentleman with white hair, walks along the Thames embankment. The moon is full, London is serene. This peace is about to be destroyed.
panels.narration: It was a fine night — the moon lay on her back, and the lanes were brilliantly lit.

panels.visual_direction: Hyde appears from shadow, cane in hand. His shadow falls over Carew. The panel is split diagonally — the peaceful moonlit half versus the encroaching crimson darkness of Hyde's arrival.

VIOLENCE — rendered almost abstractly. The cane rises and falls. Splashes of crimson against the blue moonlight. Panel borders crack and splinter. Hyde's face is pure savage joy. This should be horrifying but artfully composed — the violence of a Caravaggio painting.
panels.narration: With ape-like fury, he was trampling his victim under foot and hailing down a storm of blows.

panels.visual_direction: Aftermath: The broken cane lies in two pieces. A pool of moonlight — or is it something else? — spreads across the cobblestones. Hyde is gone. Only the fog remains.
panels.narration: The stick with which the deed had been done was of some rare and very tough wood — it had broken in the middle under the stress of this insensate cruelty.

panel_scripts.layout_notes: Build from quiet dread to the explosive revelation. The door becomes a character. Final panels should be the largest in the entire novel.

panels.visual_direction: Jekyll's butler Poole stands at Utterson's door, terror in his eyes. Behind him, the street is a wall of fog. His hands twist his hat. The warm light from Utterson's hallway contrasts with the cold night.
dialogue: Mr. Utterson, sir — something is wrong.

panels.visual_direction: Utterson and Poole approach Jekyll's laboratory door. Servants huddle in the hallway behind them, holding candles that create a procession of wavering light. The door at the end of the corridor is the darkest point in the image — a void.
dialogue: Jekyll! I demand to see you!

panels.visual_direction: A voice from behind the door — rendered as a jagged speech bubble, the lettering unstable, wavering between Jekyll's refined hand and something more primal.
panels.narration: Utterson heard a voice from within: a voice that was not Jekyll's — and yet somehow was.

panels.visual_direction: FULL PAGE: The door crashes open. Inside, Hyde's body lies crumpled on the floor, still twitching. A vial rolls from his hand. But the horror is in the details — Jekyll's clothes on Hyde's small frame. The chemicals still smoking. The full-length mirror reflecting something we cannot see. Utterson and Poole stand frozen in the doorway, backlit.
panels.narration: Right in the midst there lay the body of a man sorely contorted and still twitching. They drew near on tiptoe, turned it on its back, and beheld the face of Edward Hyde.

panel_scripts.layout_notes: The transformation sequence. Panels dissolve and morph. Jekyll's handwriting narrates. This is the emotional climax — horror and tragedy intertwined.

panels.visual_direction: Jekyll alone in his laboratory, hand reaching for a bubbling green potion. The room is cluttered with scientific apparatus. His face shows equal parts terror and fascination. The potion glows, casting his face in an eerie green light.
panels.narration: I hesitated long before I put this theory to the test of practice. I knew well that I risked death.

panels.visual_direction: THE TRANSFORMATION — a four-part sequence within one panel. Jekyll drinks. His body convulses. His features shift and compress. Hyde emerges. Each stage overlaps the last like a multiple exposure photograph. Pain and ecstasy are indistinguishable on his changing face.
panels.narration: The most racking pangs succeeded: a grinding in the bones, deadly nausea, and a horror of the spirit that cannot be exceeded at the hour of birth or death.

panels.visual_direction: Hyde stands before a full-length mirror, seeing himself for the first time. His reflection fills the panel — small, young, wicked, grinning. Behind the mirror, the ghostly outline of Jekyll watches, trapped.
panels.narration: I felt younger, lighter, happier in body. I knew myself, at the first breath of this new life, to be more wicked, tenfold more wicked — and the thought delighted me like wine.

panels.visual_direction: Final panel — split vertically. Left half: Jekyll writing his confession by candlelight, tears on his cheeks, hand trembling. Right half: Hyde's shadow looming behind him, growing, consuming. The two halves are separated by a crack that runs through the middle — the self, divided and irreparable.
panels.narration: I bring the life of that unhappy Henry Jekyll to an end.

generated_panels.image_prompt:
Wide-angle establishing shot, low camera angle looking slightly upward along a narrow Victorian London street at dusk. The perspective recedes into deep fog, creating a claustrophobic corridor of looming architecture.

Two male silhouettes dominate the lower-center foreground, walking side by side away from the viewer at a measured, contemplative pace. The taller figure — Mr. Utterson — is lean and angular in a conservative dark suit, his rugged weathered profile barely visible as a three-quarter turn. Beside him walks Mr. Enfield, similarly dressed in Victorian gentleman's attire. Both men are rendered primarily as dark shapes, their forms solid and grounded against the dissolving world around them. Utterson's posture is upright but carries the quiet weight of a man who guards too many secrets.

Flanking them on both sides, Victorian terraced buildings rise in asymmetric masses, upper stories dissolving completely into amber-tinged fog. Heavy ink-wash texture defines the stone facades — deeply shadowed recesses, ornate cornices swallowed by mist, dark windows that suggest watching rather than light. Wrought iron railings and stone steps jut from the buildings like skeletal fingers.

Three gas lamps are visible along the street — the nearest lamp casts a concentrated amber halo (#D4A847) that bleeds into the fog, creating layered rings of sickly warm light. The lamplight catches the cobblestones below in slick amber reflections, suggesting recent rain. The deeper street beyond dissolves into cool blue-grey (#6B7B8D) mist, the fog thickening with distance.

The sky above is a turbulent wash of deep charcoal (#2C2C2C) pressing down, barely distinguishable from the building tops. The overall palette is dominated by charcoal blacks and deep shadow, punctuated only by the amber gaslight and a faint ghostly ivory fog.

Shadows are exaggerated and directional in the Mignola tradition — hard-edged black pools beneath the architecture, elongated silhouettes of the two men stretching along wet cobblestones. The ink-wash texture is heavy throughout: rough, organic strokes suggesting grime and age. Cross-hatching defines architectural depth.

The composition uses the street as a vanishing-point tunnel, pulling the eye toward an obscured vanishing point swallowed in fog. The two figures are small relative to the architecture, emphasizing human insignificance against the oppressive Victorian cityscape. Atmosphere is thick with dread despite the mundane act of an evening walk — the fog itself feels animate, concealing rather than merely obscuring.

Art style: Dark Victorian noir graphic novel, heavy ink-wash textures, deep shadow masses, influenced by Mike Mignola and Dave McKean. High contrast. Painterly but graphic. No text, no lettering, no captions, no speech bubbles, no words of any kind anywhere in the image.

generated_panels.image_prompt:
Medium shot, slightly low angle, two-thirds frame composition. A well-dressed Victorian gentleman — Mr. Enfield, a trim man in his thirties wearing a dark overcoat and top hat, ruddy-cheeked from a late-night walk — stands on a fog-wrapped London street, his right arm extended, one gloved finger pointing toward a door set flush into a long, bare, windowless wall to his left. His posture holds a tension between casual storytelling and involuntary unease, his body angled slightly away from the door even as he gestures at it, as though reluctant to fully face it.

The door dominates the left side of the frame. It is a battered, low, two-panelled door of no architectural distinction — its paint blistered and peeling in leprous patches, its wood grain stained dark with age and damp, its brass knocker tarnished to near-black. It sits recessed slightly into the wall, and the shadows at its threshold are unnaturally deep, pooling like ink that refuses to drain, as though the darkness behind it presses outward. The wall itself is plain, the surrounding buildings respectable and well-maintained Victorian terraces — which makes the door's presence feel deeply, inexplicably wrong. A single gaslight on a wrought-iron post further down the street bleeds sickly amber (#D4A847) across the cobblestones, casting long distorted shadows that stretch toward the door like fingers.

The fog is thick but low — a Victorian pea-souper clinging to the wet cobblestones, swallowing the bases of the buildings. Wisps of mist curl around Enfield's boots and drift toward the door's threshold, as if drawn inward. The overall palette is deep charcoal (#2C2C2C) with amber gaslight picking out Enfield's coat and the wet stones, cold blue-grey (#6B7B8D) bleeding into the mid-distance fog. The door itself sits in its own shadow, neither amber nor blue — an absence of both.

Art style: Dark Victorian noir with heavy ink wash textures in the manner of Mike Mignola and Dave McKean. Deep, confident blacks with crosshatched shadow work. Linework that is deliberate and bold, with watercolor-wash tones bleeding at the edges. The shadows around the door's threshold are rendered as solid black shapes with no interior detail — pure absence. Gaslight halos are soft, amber, impressionistic. The overall mood is oppressive Victorian dread: the feeling that the door is not merely old and ugly, but wrong in some way that bypasses rational thought and registers only as instinctive revulsion. No text, no lettering, no signage, no captions, no speech bubbles of any kind.
generated_panels.alt_text: Medium shot of Enfield gesturing toward a sinister door set into a windowless wall. The door is blistered, stained — utterly out of place on the respectable street. Deep shadows pool around its threshold.

generated_panels.image_prompt:
Graphic novel panel, dark Victorian noir ink wash illustration, Mike Mignola and Dave McKean style. Tilted Dutch angle composition, approximately 15 degrees clockwise, creating disorientation and dread. The frame is tight and claustrophobic.

COMPOSITION: Low-angle shot from ground level, looking up from the cobblestones. The focal point is Hyde's boot mid-stride, planted callously against the cobblestones beside a small child's splayed hand. The scene is framed by the sharp corner of two narrow Victorian street walls converging in the background, forcing the eye toward the act of violence at center.

CHARACTERS: Hyde — a small, pale, dwarfish male figure in the middle distance, rendered almost entirely in silhouette and deep shadow. His face is completely obscured beneath the brim of a heavy cape collar and hat, swallowed by darkness. Despite his diminutive stature, his silhouette dominates the panel — his shadow cast by a distant gaslight stretches grotesquely long and wide across the wet cobblestones, three times larger than his body, distorted into something monstrous. His posture is chillingly upright, unhurried — one foot mid-step, spine straight, radiating cold indifference rather than rage. Jekyll's oversized clothes hang loose from his smaller frame, cape billowing. A fallen child in white dress is crumpled at the street corner, small pale limbs against dark wet stone, mouth open in a silent cry. The child rendered in ivory white (#F5F0E1), a stark contrast to the surrounding darkness.

ENVIRONMENT: A narrow Victorian London street corner at night. Wet cobblestones slick with rain, reflecting distorted amber and crimson light. A single gaslight at the far end of the lane casts a sickly amber (#D4A847) cone of light that barely reaches the scene, leaving most of the panel in deep charcoal shadow (#2C2C2C). The surrounding architecture — brick walls, iron railings, a dark doorway — presses inward. Wisps of fog curl low along the ground. The laboratory door is faintly visible in deep shadow in the far background, barely discernible.

COLOR TREATMENT: Near-monochromatic, dominated by blood crimson (#8B0000) bleeding across the cobblestones and saturating Hyde's shadow like a stain. Deep charcoal blacks form the majority of the frame. Sparse amber touches on the distant gaslight only. The child's dress is the sole ivory white element, fragile and isolated. This is a flashback panel — the entire image has a slight vignette burn at the edges, as if viewed through corrupted memory.

STYLE: Heavy ink wash, cross-hatched shadows, expressionist distortion on architecture. Brushwork is rough and violent at the edges, precise only on Hyde's silhouette. No halftones — pure shadow and light. Oppressive, nightmarish quality. No text, letters, captions, symbols, or speech bubbles anywhere in the image.

generated_panels.image_prompt:
Extreme close-up shot, the entire panel consumed by a single massive Victorian door, filling the frame edge to edge with oppressive, looming presence. The door is ancient, thick-planked wood of deep charcoal black, the grain running vertically like claw marks etched into the surface over decades. Within the wood grain itself, the natural patterns subtly suggest a contorted face — hollow eye sockets formed by dark knots, a gaping mouth implied by a long split in the timber, not overtly literal but deeply unsettling, the kind of shape the brain recognizes before the eye does.

At the center of the frame, slightly below the midpoint, a brass keyhole plate catches a sliver of amber gaslight from somewhere off-panel to the lower left. The keyhole itself glints with a cold, singular yellow-gold gleam — shaped like an eye, vertical and watchful, the only source of warm light in an otherwise dead-black composition. The surrounding metal is tarnished and pitted, ringed with age and grime.

In the polished upper wood, barely perceptible — a ghost of a reflection: the elongated, distorted silhouette of Mr. Gabriel Utterson. His lean, dark-suited form is rendered in cold blue-grey tones within the reflection, fragmented across the uneven grain, his deep-set watchful eyes just barely resolving out of the distortion. He appears small, swallowed by the door's mass, a man confronting something far larger than himself. His reflected face carries no expression — only stillness.

The door's iron hinges are massive, rusted to near-black, barely clinging to a crumbling brick surround at the panel edges. No door handle is visible — this is a door that does not invite entry. A thin hairline crack of absolute darkness runs along the bottom edge — nothing beyond it, only void.

Lighting is almost entirely absent except for the keyhole's amber glint and a faint blue-grey ambient glow catching the edge of Utterson's reflection. Shadows are Mignola-heavy — inky, flat, with crisp geometric edges that feel more drawn than rendered. Texture is McKean ink-wash, the wood built from layered charcoal strokes and bleed marks, tactile and gritty.

Color palette: dominant deep charcoal (#2C2C2C), with the single sickly amber (#D4A847) keyhole gleam, cold blue-grey (#6B7B8D) in the reflection, and traces of ivory white only in the faint highlight catching the door's upper edge. The grain suggests blood crimson in the deepest shadow pockets — subliminal, not literal.

Mood: pure Victorian dread. A threshold between worlds. The door is not haunted — the door IS the haunting.

Art style: dark graphic novel illustration, Mike Mignola ink-block shadows, Dave McKean mixed-media texture, high contrast, no text, no lettering, no speech bubbles, no captions.
generated_panels.alt_text: Close-up of the sinister door, now filling the entire panel. The wood grain seems to form a face. A keyhole glints like an eye. Utterson's reflection is barely visible in the dark wood.

generated_panels.image_prompt:
Close-up medium shot, slightly low angle, centered on a lean weathered man seated at a heavy Victorian writing desk. The frame is intimate and oppressive — walls feel close, ceiling lost to darkness above.

SUBJECT: Gabriel Utterson, a lean, long-faced lawyer with a rugged, deeply lined face carved by decades of keeping secrets. Deep-set watchful eyes cast downward, brow furrowed with quiet dread. Firm jaw tightened. He wears a conservative dark charcoal suit, perfectly proper but swallowed by shadow. Both hands hold a single document at chest level — a legal parchment that catches all available light, glowing a warm amber-gold from the single candle flame burning low on the desk beside him. His fingers grip the edges of the document with restrained urgency. His expression is troubled, still, like a man who has read something he cannot unread.

LIGHTING: Singular candlelight source from the desk, casting amber (#D4A847) warmth across the document and the lower half of Utterson's face. His forehead and the tops of his cheekbones fall into deep charcoal shadow (#2C2C2C). The flame is small, barely holding against the weight of the darkness surrounding it. No secondary light sources — the room is sealed in night.

ENVIRONMENT: A Victorian bachelor's study, dense with brooding atmosphere. Behind Utterson, floor-to-ceiling bookshelves recede steeply into absolute darkness — spines of leather-bound volumes visible only closest to the candle, fading to silhouette, then to nothing. The desk is heavy dark wood, cluttered edges vanishing into shadow. No windows visible — the night is implied rather than shown. The room feels airtight, suffocating, the darkness pressing inward like a living thing.

ATMOSPHERE: Still, oppressive Victorian dread. The shadows are not passive — they lean. Ink wash textures layer across every surface: hatching on the suit, pooled black in the corners of the room, textured grain on the bookshelves. The amber glow of the document feels sickly, a warmth that unsettles rather than comforts — light the color of moral corruption.

STYLE: Dark Victorian noir rendered in heavy ink wash, deep shadow masses with minimal linework visible. Influences of Mike Mignola's blocked shadow work and Dave McKean's textural atmospheric depth. Color palette strictly limited: deep charcoal dominates, sickly amber illuminates only the document and Utterson's central face, cold blue-grey (#6B7B8D) bleeds faintly into the shadow edges of the bookshelves. No crimson present — Hyde is absent from this moment. High contrast. Painterly. Heavy. No text, no lettering, no words, no captions, no speech bubbles anywhere in the image.

MOOD: Isolation and foreboding. A man confronting a truth in silence. The document is the only light in the world.

generated_panels.image_prompt:
Triptych composition, three vertical frames side by side within a single panel, each depicting the same narrow Victorian cobblestone alley at different times of day. The frames share a continuous background — the same recessed doorway, the same gas lamp post, the same damp stone walls — but the light and shadow shift dramatically across each frame.

**Left frame — Dawn:** Cold blue-grey light bleeds over fog-drenched cobblestones. Utterson stands motionless to the left of the doorway, a lean, long figure in a conservative dark suit and weathered overcoat, collar turned up against the chill. His deep-set eyes are fixed on the door. A single gas lamp still burns amber, fighting the pale morning. Fog pools at his feet. The street is deserted. His shadow stretches thin and long behind him.

**Center frame — Noon:** Flat, joyless grey light — no warmth, no color — washes the alley. Utterson occupies the same position, same posture, slightly more rigid. His face is turned three-quarters toward the door, jaw firm, watchful eyes patient and unblinking. A few distant pedestrian silhouettes blur in the background fog, but none approach the door. The gaslight is extinguished. Shadows retreat but never fully vanish — they pool in doorframes and under eaves.

**Right frame — Night:** Gaslight returns, casting a sickly amber corona on wet cobblestones. The door is swallowed in deep charcoal shadow. Utterson now stands closer, half-consumed by darkness himself, only the amber highlight of his rugged jaw and the gleam of his watchful eyes catching the light. Fog thickens into near-opacity. His shadow on the wall behind him is massive, distorted, doubling his silhouette like a second figure. The street is utterly empty. The recessed laboratory door looms at the edge of frame, a threshold into absolute blackness.

Across all three frames, the doorway anchors the right edge — identical, unchanging, perpetually in shadow. The repetition of Utterson's silhouette creates a sentinel rhythm. Heavy ink wash textures roughen the stone walls. Cross-hatched shadows deepen with each frame. Color palette: deep charcoal dominates, sickly amber gaslight punctuates the dawn and night frames, cold blue-grey drains the noon frame of life.

Art style: Dark Victorian noir, Mike Mignola-influenced heavy shadow blocking with Dave McKean ink wash texture. Thick expressive linework. Fog rendered as translucent layered washes. Atmosphere oppressive and claustrophobic — the street a cage Utterson willingly inhabits. Mood: obsessive vigilance, creeping dread, the weight of a secret not yet known but already felt. No figures other than Utterson. No text, no lettering, no speech bubbles, no captions.

generated_panels.image_prompt:
Low-angle wide shot framed in a narrow cobblestone alleyway at night. A weathered wooden door fills the left third of the composition, thrown open mid-frame. Hyde stands in the doorway threshold, body half-swallowed by the deep charcoal interior darkness behind him — only the right side of his face illuminated by a distant amber gaslight at the end of the alley. His face is pale, almost cadaverous, features unsettlingly proportioned — not deformed, but fundamentally wrong. Jekyll's oversized frock coat hangs loose on his dwarfish frame, sleeves too long, shoulders slumped with excess fabric. A heavy dark cape drapes around him. His unsettling smile catches the gaslight like a blade. His shadow stretches tall and distorted behind him on the door, grotesquely larger than his small body — a silhouette that does not match the man.

Utterson stands in the foreground, center-right, a full head taller than Hyde. His back is three-quarters to the viewer, lean frame in a conservative dark suit and greatcoat, the muted browns and reliable grey of his clothing absorbing the fog. His posture is rigid, blocking Hyde's exit — but something in the set of his shoulders, the almost imperceptible lean backward, suggests instinctive recoil. Despite his height advantage, Utterson is clearly the one made vulnerable by this encounter. His deep-set eyes are fixed on Hyde's face with grim watchful intensity. His firm jaw is set.

The environment is a cramped Soho side-street — narrow, wet cobblestones reflecting the amber gaslight as sickly pools. Thick Victorian fog rolls in from the background, obscuring the gas lamp into a diffused amber halo. Brick walls press in on both sides, slick with damp. The door Hyde occupies is scarred and discolored, the threshold itself shadowed as a threshold between worlds.

Lighting is dramatic chiaroscuro: warm amber gaslight from behind Utterson illuminates his back and casts his shadow forward across Hyde, while the interior darkness behind Hyde provides total black negative space. Hyde's half-lit face sits precisely on the light-shadow boundary. Blood crimson bleeds into the scene as subtle color grading around Hyde's silhouette and in the shadows at his feet.

Art style references Mike Mignola's heavy ink blacks and Dave McKean's textured, painterly atmosphere — bold shadow shapes, minimal mid-tones, ink wash grain throughout. The composition creates claustrophobic dread: two figures, tight alley, fog closing in. Hyde looks up at Utterson with that wrong smile. The size difference is undeniable. The power dynamic is reversed. Mood: predatory stillness beneath a veneer of civility, the monstrous hidden in plain sight.

editorial_review.visual_consistency: Strong noir aesthetic maintained throughout. The gaslight-to-moonlight color shifting is effective. Hyde's consistent small stature creates excellent visual dissonance.
editorial_review.narrative_coherence: The five selected scenes create a compelling arc from mystery to revelation. The Carew murder scene effectively marks the turn from suspense to horror.
editorial_review.dialogue_quality: Dialogue is well-adapted from the source — concise and powerful. The mix of original Stevenson prose in narration with adapted dialogue works well.
editorial_review.pacing: Excellent build from slow-burn suspense to explosive revelation. The transformation sequence is the emotional peak, properly positioned.
issues: Scene 3 panel 3 could be more specific about composition to ensure the violence reads as artistic rather than gratuitous
Consider adding a quiet epilogue panel after the full statement — Utterson alone with the letter
suggestions: The color palette could incorporate more green for the transformation scenes to contrast with the amber/crimson palette
Consider a recurring visual motif of hands — Jekyll's refined hands becoming Hyde's brutal ones
editorial_review.summary: A strong, atmospheric adaptation that captures the psychological horror of Stevenson's novella. The visual style guide creates a cohesive world, and the scene selection balances suspense, violence, and tragedy effectively. Approved with minor suggestions for enhancement.
